Some bat species are also the reservoir hosts of zoonoses that have severe human health consequences (rabies, Nipah, Marburg) and others have been implicated in the emergence of the human pathogenic coronaviruses SARS, Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), and now SARS-CoV-2 []. This duality has led to entrenched positions within the bat and virus research communities, with accusations of alarmist risk inflation to support funding of viral discovery on the one hand and denial or down-playing of the role of bats in emerging infectious diseases on the other. Media representation has further polarized positions, with emotive headlines that refer to bats as, for example, “breeding grounds of deadly diseases” (https://www.discovermagazine.com/health/why-bats-are-breeding-grounds-for-deadly-diseases-like-ebola-and-sars) or “the number-one carrier of disease” (https://time.com/4827511/bats-viruses-diseases-pandemic/).

The consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic for human health are apparent, but negative outcomes for bat populations and conservation are also concerning. Bat conservation has always been challenged by public perceptions of bats, but the misperception that bats carry the circulating pandemic strain of SARS-CoV-2 has led to lethal persecution [], evictions from roosts, and has compromised existing conservation programs []. Moreover, there is a small but credible risk that SARS-CoV-2 could be transmitted from humans to bats, with unknown consequences for bat health []. Thus, SARS-CoV-2 threatens both human and bat health, but advancing the missions of bat conservation and public health protection has seemed, to many, to conflict, hampering the integrative research needed to characterize and mitigate disease emergence.

To investigate cross-disciplinary collaboration between ecological- and infectious disease-oriented bat researchers, we undertook a bibliometric analysis of coauthor relationships. Publication metadata were extracted from the Web of Science database on over 5,600 journal articles published between 1950 and 2019 (see S1 Text). Consistent with the divisions observed between ecology, veterinary, and other professionals working in a broader One Health context [], our analysis revealed a clear boundary between authors representing disease- and ecology-focused disciplines in bat research (Fig 1) and distinct clusters within disciplines. Discipline-specific expertise is the bedrock of collaborative research, so disciplinary clusters of productive research groups are expected and needed []. Eighteen highly connected, influential authors were identified (betweenness centrality >500), but only nine published with colleagues outside their primary discipline (Fig 1: Authors “A” from disease and “B” from ecology). Moreover, five of these nine “boundary-crossing” authors came from the same cluster containing author “B” (Fig 1). Other influential authors, while extraordinarily productive within their own fields, have not published outside of their discipline (Fig 1: Authors “C” in disease and “D” in ecology).

Fig 1. Coauthorship network of the 200 most-published bat researchers between 1950 and 2019.
Map shows location of institutional affiliations of authors in each cluster. Colors correspond to the author network clusters; squares denote apparent segregation of research groups geographically in addition to topic area. Inset shows the publication networks of four influential authors with betweenness centrality scores >500. Authors "A" and "B" are boundary-crossing authors with collaboration networks that span clusters in both ecology and disease topic areas. Authors "C" and "D" are widely connected within either the ecology or disease communities but do not collaborate across disciplines. Clustering was also driven by geographical and institutional boundaries associated with programmatic missions or funding (inset map) promoting homogenous perspectives within the cluster and potentially retarding dissemination of findings. See S1 Text for additional detail on this analysis. This figure was created with permission using BioRender.com. WNS, White Nose Syndrome.

 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000947.g001

So how can we increase connectivity and strengthen the network? Our analysis highlighted the power of a common goal to overcome institutional, cultural and trust barriers and accelerate interdisciplinary collaboration [,]. This was exemplified by an international cluster focused on White Nose Syndrome (WNS) (blue/orange in Fig 1), a disease resulting from a fungal pathogen that has killed millions of bats in North America since it was first detected in 2006. The WNS cluster repeatedly crosses disciplinary lines in the network, and its diverse membership produced interdisciplinary papers that combined principles of ecology with those of infectious disease to address themes relevant to the study of disease emergence in any pathogen system, e.g., host/pathogen interactions, pathogen transmission in community networks, disease effects on macroecological patterns of bats, invasion ecology, seasonal transmission dynamics, and transcriptomics (see S1 Data).

Just as WNS provides common ground for convergent research, understanding and mitigating other emerging zoonoses with One Health implications, like SARS-CoV-2, involve common challenges that are best met through cross-disciplinary engagement. This engagement can span robust data collection for a complementary discipline (leveraging), interdisciplinary projects designed collaboratively from the ground up (building), and research networks that actively aim to integrate domains and resources (networking):

Leveraging existing research programs can further common agendas. For example, characterizing the distribution of bat diversity and resolving taxonomic questions is both central to effective bat conservation [] and needed to draw correct associations between pathogens and hosts. Many viral discovery/surveillance papers do not identify bat hosts to the species level, in part because bat diversity of many regions of biosurveillance interest is poorly known, with unresolved taxonomy of species-rich groups, cryptic species complexes, and likely many undescribed species. Surveillance teams can lever their programs to contribute and benefit by doing the following: i) integrating biodiversity expertise (ecologists, taxonomists, etc.) and infrastructure into the team from the outset [] (this would facilitate species identifications and robust integration of ecological principles into study design); ii) sequencing tissues collected for pathogen detection for host species markers and contributing to reference databases (currently, > 800 bat species are represented in the Barcode of Life Database [BOLD] of DNA sequences matched to identified voucher specimens); and iii) depositing voucher specimens with curated collections (prioritizing in-country national or university collections). Preservation of the cold chain in surveillance work presents an unparalleled opportunity for disease teams to contribute high-quality (flash-frozen) material to the global effort to sequence the full genome of all living bat species (Bat 1K— https://bat1k.ucd.ie/), an initiative that is already paying dividends for understanding tolerance to viral infection in bats [].

Building new integrative research areas that are foundational to both research domains provides strong motivation for collaboration. The question “What is a sick bat?” is central to global discussion of the ability of bats to harbor infectious agents that are highly pathogenic to people but with (usually) little apparent health impact to themselves (reviewed by []). Understanding bat health may provide important biomedical insights regarding infection tolerance. Bat health is also a key concept in studies of anthropogenic and environmental stressors that both threaten species conservation [] and influence pathogen shedding and infection dynamics [,]. Similarly, human–bat interactions, such as bat hunting and consumption, are relevant to both bat conservation and cross-species transmission of pathogens and would benefit from greater integrative effort to characterize the intersection of bat biology and ecology (e.g., bat movement, reproductive phenology, and resource availability), drivers of human behavior (e.g., economics, seasonality, attitudes, and social norms) and disease dynamics. There is extensive guidance on the development of interdisciplinary teams and research in the literature [,], but the critical first step is for experts in different domains to network and build professional relationships based on mutual understanding and trust [].

Networking individuals and existing networks builds and reinforces relationships that accelerate the transfer of knowledge and expertise and allow for coordination of activities and key resources []. Many ecologists within our coauthor network have access to long-term study sites or wild study populations, key resources with years and sometimes decades of relevant data on ecology, life history, genetic relationships, responses to disturbance regimes, etc. These established sites and populations could provide settings for pathogen studies across ecological and conservation contexts. Conversely, numerous scientific questions can only be rigorously addressed with the use of captive bat colonies. Such colonies are few but distributed across the coauthor network in support of research that ranges from the biomechanics of flight and the evolution of sociality to experimental challenges with infectious agents to determine susceptibility and disease dynamics relevant to human or bat health. Ideally, networking of existing colonies could facilitate access to representatives from each bat family, comparison of biological phenomena across taxa, and generation of associated primary cell lines, genomic data, and transcriptomic data. While there is clear potential for colonies held for nondisease research to make noninvasive or minimally invasive contributions to a network of colonies, this can be a contentious issue that is most likely to be advanced in a network that has established trust and respect among members.

We invite readers to join the Bat One Health Research Network (BOHRN) (https://www.bohrn.net/), an initiative established in 2017 to bring together disease and bat researchers to characterize global threats of bat-borne pathogens in a conservation-conscious One Health framework. Efforts focus on the following: host–pathogen interactions; pathogen surveillance, diagnostics, and epidemiology; bat ecology in natural and human-modified landscapes; and human–bat interactions. BOHRN members include ecologists, conservation biologists, immunologists, virologists, veterinary scientists, and modelers. To facilitate network building and enable researchers to connect with complementary experts, members have access to a membership directory and receive notification of BOHRN events, funding opportunities, conferences receptive to interdisciplinary or cross-disciplinary presentations, and symposia. The diverse global membership is committed to the development of more transparent, open, and collaborative research and practices and is invited to contribute to or join the working groups addressing the thematic foci that establish our common ground.

title: Physiological and gene expression analysis of Hevea brasiliensis under drought stress
content:
Abstract
Natural rubber, derived mainly from the Hevea brasiliensis tree, is a highly valuable biopolymer. This study examined the effects of drought stress on rubber seedlings, focusing on their physiological responses and gene expression under three irrigation conditions: well-watered (control), mild drought, and severe drought. Results indicated that as drought severity increased, the relative water content in the leaves decreased. The level of proline was significantly higher under severe drought but decreased during mild drought stress. Malondialdehyde levels increased in leaves under drought stress, while antioxidant enzymes varied: ascorbate peroxidase and catalase activity increased under mild drought stress. The guaiacol peroxidase (GPX) activity rose under drought condition, indicating adaptive oxidative and osmotic responses. Gene expression analysis demonstrated significant down-regulation of the rubber biosynthesis gene 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGR) under drought conditions, indicating a reduction in rubber production. In contrast, the expression of cis-prenyltransferase was up-regulated, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to maintain rubber synthesis despite a shortage of precursors. HMG-CoA synthase significantly decreased under severe drought stress, whereas transferase activator exhibited non-significant changes during drought conditions. Additionally, an inverse relationship was identified between HMGR expression and GPX activity, suggesting that increased levels of reactive oxygen species during drought stress may inhibit antioxidant responses, ultimately leading to the down-regulation of HMGR. Drought stress suppresses HMGR expression, reducing rubber yield. Preventing the downregulation of this gene under drought conditions could be a key focus for future research. These findings enhance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of drought adaptation in rubber seedlings and provide insights for breeding resilient genotypes.

Citation: Mohammadi Nodehi M, Mahmoudieh M, Taleei A, Mohammadi V, Rahman MM, Zargar M, et al. (2025) Physiological and gene expression analysis of Hevea brasiliensis under drought stress. PLoS One 20(12):
 e0338177.

 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0338177
Editor: Mojtaba Kordrostami, Nuclear Science and Technology Research Institute, IRAN, ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF
Received: August 29, 2025; Accepted: November 18, 2025; Published: December 30, 2025

Data Availability: All relevant data are within the paper and its Supporting Information files.
Funding: The author(s) received no specific funding for this work.
Competing interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

Introduction
Natural rubber (NR), mainly composed of cis-1,4-polyisoprene, is a crucial biopolymer used in industries like automotive, medical, and manufacturing []. Although over 2,500 plant species produce rubber [], only Hevea brasiliensis is commercially viable, supplying about 89% of global natural rubber [,,]. In rubber seedlings, rubber biosynthesis occurs in specialized cells called articulated laticifers, primarily located in the phloem of stems, with some in leaves and branches [–]. These cells generate latex, a cytoplasmic suspension rich in rubber particles and enzymes for the isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway [,].

The rubber synthesis pathway is energy intensive and particularly sensitive to ecological stress conditions []. Due to increasing climatic instability, understanding responses of rubber seedlings to environmental stress is essential for establishing long-term productivity. Drought stress is a major global constraint that increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inhibits respiration, partially due to reduced antioxidants []. Enzymes such as ascorbate peroxidase (APX), catalase (CAT), and guaiacol peroxidase (GPX) play key roles in detoxifying ROS and protecting plants from oxidative damage []. However, excessive ROS can hinder crop productivity by inducing physiological disruptions such as membrane lipid peroxidation, protein misfolding, and metabolite degradation [,]. This study aims to investigate the effects of drought on growth traits, antioxidant enzyme activities, osmolyte accumulation, and expression of four key genes (HMGR, HMGS, RTA, and CPT) involved in rubber biosynthesis [,]. Elucidating these factors will enhance our understanding of the mechanisms behind drought tolerance in rubber seedlings. This knowledge will support future breeding and cultivation efforts under drought-prone conditions.

Materials and methods

Plant material, experimental design, and growth conditions

Seeds of the rubber tree (clone RRIB-600) were soaked in water for 24 hours at room temperature and then sown in black polyethylene nursery bags filled with washed river sand. The seeds were lightly covered with sand and kept in a greenhouse at 28–30 °C with humidity above 60%, with daily watering to maintain soil moisture. Seed germination was observed between 13 and 17 days after sowing. Eight-week-old seedlings, approximately 25 cm long, were transplanted into plastic pots containing a loamy-sandy textured substrate. The plants were grown in a controlled greenhouse environment with temperatures between 28 and 30 °C, relative humidity levels of 60–70%, and a 12-hour light/dark photoperiod. Six-month-old seedlings (15 seedlings) were selected for morphological assessment, with five biological replicates (n = 5) per treatment group (each pot representing a separate biological replicate). A summary of the experimental design is illustrated in Fig 1.

Drought stress treatments and morphological assessment

Six-month-old rubber seedlings were subjected to drought treatments for 42 days using fixed daily irrigation volumes methods as previously described [,]. In brief, they received 50 mL/day for the well-watered control, 20 mL/day for mild drought stress, and 2 mL/day for severe stress. Irrigation was performed manually every 2–3 days to ensure consistent water delivery.

Morphological evaluations were conducted at the beginning and end of the treatment period, measuring plant height and stem diameter. At the end of treatments, fully expanded leaves were harvested, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at –80 °C for biochemical and molecular analyses.

Physiological assays

Relative water content (RWC).
RWC was estimated as described previously [,]. Briefly, the fresh weight (FW) was measured immediately after sampling from each plant. The leaves were then floated in distilled water for 6 hours, and the turgid weight (TW) was recorded. Afterward, the leaves were oven-dried at 70°C for 48 hours, and the dry weight (DW) was determined. The RWC was calculated using the following formula []:

Proline quantification.
Free proline was extracted and quantified using the acid ninhydrin method [,]. Briefly, 0.5 g of frozen leaf tissue was homogenized in 10 mL of 3% sulfosalicylic acid and vortexed for 30 seconds. The mixture was then centrifuged (Sigma Qiagen Model 4–16KS, Germany) at 22,500 xg for 15 minutes at 4°C. The supernatant was filtered through filter paper. 2 mL of the filtrate were mixed with 2 mL of acid ninhydrin and 2 mL of glacial acetic acid, then incubated at 65°C for 1 hour and cooled on ice. The chromophore was extracted with 4 mL of toluene, and the absorbance of the upper phase (colored solution) was read at 520 nm using a plate reader (EON Biotek, Highland Park, Winooski, Vermont, USA). Concentrations were determined from a standard curve of pure proline, expressed as micrograms per gram of dry weight.

Malondialdehyde (MDA) content.
MDA, a marker of lipid peroxidation, was measured using the thiobarbituric acid (TBA) assay []. 1 g of fresh leaf tissue was homogenized in 5 mL of 0.1% trichloroacetic acid (TCA), followed by centrifugation at 10,000 xg for 5 minutes at room temperature. 1 mL of the supernatant was mixed with 4 mL of 20% TCA containing 0.5% TBA and incubated at 95°C for 30 minutes. After cooling on ice and re-centrifugation, absorbance was measured at 532 nm and 600 nm. The MDA content was calculated using an extinction coefficient of 155 mM ⁻ ¹cm ⁻ ¹.

Antioxidant enzyme assays

For enzyme assays, 0.2 g of leaf tissue was homogenized in 1 mL of extraction buffer containing 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 6.8) and 2% polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). Samples were vortexed for 30 seconds and centrifuged at 22,500 xg for 30 minutes at 4°C []. Supernatants were collected and stored at –20°C until analysis.

Catalase (CAT) activity was assayed by measuring the decomposition of 50 mM H₂O₂ in 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0). An aliquot (10 μL) of enzyme extract was mixed with reaction buffer at a dilution ratio of 1:200, and the decrease in absorbance was recorded at 240 nm [,].

To assess ascorbate peroxidase (APX) activity a reaction mixture containing 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), 0.5 mM ascorbate, and 1 mM H₂O₂ was prepared []. The APX activity was measured by monitoring the decrease in absorbance at 290 nm for 2 minutes. The activity was expressed as ΔA 290 mg −1 protein min −1.

Guaiacol Peroxidase (GPX) activity was determined by measuring the formation of tetra guaiacol, which absorbs at 470 nm []. Equal volumes of 10 mM phosphate buffer, guaiacol (10 mM), and H₂O₂ were mixed. The enzyme extract was added to the mixture at a dilution ratio of 1:200. The increase in absorbance was recorded over 2 minutes at 470 nm.

Quantitative real-time PCR analysis

Total RNA was extracted from approximately 100 mg of frozen leaf tissue using the DenaZist Total RNA kit (DenaZist, Iran), following the manufacturer’s instructions for non-column-based RNA isolation. The RNA was quantified with a Nanodrop spectrophotometer and assessed using 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. DNase treatment was then performed using the DNase I enzyme kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) to eliminate any residual genomic DNA contamination. Reverse transcription was conducted using a Supra cDNA Synthesis Kit (Pars Tous, Iran) to convert RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA). The following combinations of forward and reverse primers were used: for the quantitative real-time PCR for CPT 5′-TGTCATAGCTTCTCGCCCAA-3′/5′-ATGGTGACGTACTTAACTCCGAT-3′; for HMGR 5′-CCGTTTTCAACAAATCAAGCCGAT-3′/5′-ACCATGTTCATCCCCATTGCATC-3′; for HMGS 5′-CCATAGGACTCGCACAAGATTGC-3′/5′-GATTACCGTTTCACTCCCGACTTC-3′; and for RTA 5′-CGGACCCCAGAAGATTTATCGC-3′/5′-CTCTCCACCACAATTCCAAGATA-3′ []. The quantitative real-time PCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix (Pars Tous, Iran) in a Rotor-Gene 6000 series system (QIAGEN’s real-time PCR system), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The PCR conditions included: 95°C for 15 minutes, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 seconds; 60–62°C (depending on the annealing temperature) for 20 seconds; and 72°C for 20 seconds.

Statistical analysis

A factorial experiment based on a completely randomized design was conducted with 5 replicates. Data analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA with SAS software (version 9.4), and a p-value of 0.05 was used to determine statistical significance. The 2-ΔΔCT method [] was applied to analyze the relative expression levels of each selected gene with three technical replicates. Graphs were plotted using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0).

Results

Morphological and physiological responses to drought stress

Drought stress significantly impacted all measured morphological traits of rubber seedlings. The results showed that plant height decreased under drought conditions. Well-watered (control) plants had an average growth of 2.7 ± 1.12 cm, while mild and severe drought conditions resulted in only 0.6 ± 0.73 cm and 0.2 ± 0.4 cm growth, respectively. Stem diameter increased under severe drought (0.154 ± 0.029 mm) compared to mild drought stress (0.088 ± 0.081 mm) and control (0.24 ± 0.076 mm) (Fig 2).

Expression of genes relevant to rubber biosynthesis

The results showed that the expression patterns of genes involved in rubber biosynthesis were significantly altered by drought stress: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGR) expression declined under stress compared to well-watered (control) plants. While it decreased to 0.19 ± 0.068 in mild drought stress and further to 0.055 ± 0.012 in severe stress, indicating repression of upstream isoprenoid biosynthesis. HMG-CoA synthase (HMGS) expression significantly decreased under severe drought stress (0.79 ± 0.051), while it showed a slight increase in response to mild drought stress (1.05 ± 0.064); however, this increase was not statistically significant. The expression of the rubber transferase activator (RTA), which activates cis-prenyltransferase [], was downregulated from 1 in the control to 0.65 ± 0.26 and 0.67 ± 0.28 under mild and severe stress, respectively; however, these changes were not statistically significant. Cis-prenyltransferase (CPT), a crucial enzyme involved in polymer elongation [], demonstrated a significant upregulation under severe stress condition (3.17 ± 0.62) (Fig 4).

Discussion
This study demonstrates a closely coordinated and complex response of rubber seedlings to increasing drought stress, involving changes in morphology, function, and gene expression. The drought simulation method, which employed a controlled and gradual reduction in watering, successfully created distinct stress levels, as confirmed by significant differences in relative water content (RWC) among treatments (p < 0.05). Table 1 summarizes the ANOVA results, showing that drought treatments significantly influenced most measured traits and supporting further analysis.

Conclusion
This study provides valuable insights into the physiological and molecular responses of rubber seedlings (H. brasiliensis) to drought conditions. Our findings demonstrate that drought stress significantly impacts the relative water content, proline accumulation, and oxidative stress levels in rubber seedlings, highlighting the challenges of water scarcity. Changes in antioxidant enzyme activities, particularly ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and guaiacol peroxidase, reveal the complexity of the seedlings’ adaptive mechanisms to oxidative stress. Gene expression analysis indicates critical regulatory shifts in key biosynthetic pathways under drought. The down-regulation of the HMGR gene suggests a direct impact on rubber production, while the up-regulation of the CPT gene indicates a compensatory mechanism to sustain rubber synthesis despite precursor limitations. The inverse relationship between HMGR expression and guaiacol peroxidase activity demonstrates the balance between reactive oxygen species and antioxidant responses during drought stress. These findings enhance our understanding of drought adaptation in rubber seedlings and provide valuable information for future studies on resilient genotypes, promoting sustainable rubber production and laying a foundation for further research on drought resilience in rubber trees and related species.

title: A systematic review of water treatment with Moringa oleifera seeds: Comparative analysis of jar testing methodologies and results
content:
Abstract
This systematic review aims to assess the reliability of contemporary research on water treatment with Moringa oleifera seeds. Academic databases were browsed on a yearly basis (2014 – 2024); identification and screening were conducted between July 17th 2023 and December 9th 2024. Primary research reports featuring jar testing with M. oleifera seed coagulant were included for data collection. Thirty-five fields were used to collect data. Data was synthesised by establishing causality between independent variables and outcomes. Conflict of interest, research quality and risk of bias were assessed using modified Cochrane tools. Fifty non-duplicate publications were identified. Of these, 25 were included for data collection. In total, 511 data points were collected and synthesised. No conflicts of interest were found. Sixteen reports received “lower” or “lowest” research quality judgements. Six reports received “high risk of bias” judgements. Bias risk was most commonly associated with experimental design and missing data. Inadequate standardisation in test water preparation, M. oleifera seed coagulant processing and jar test parameters affected treatment efficacies in unpredictable ways. Researchers who used M. oleifera seed coagulants at appropriate concentrations and adhered to the three-stage model of coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation achieved turbidity reduction rates of 80–96%. Turbidity and microbiological reduction rates were comparable in three reports, but microbiological testing was uncommon. Based on their properties, M. oleifera cationic proteins are theorised to be lectins with hevein-like binding domains. These findings are significant because this technology has been in development for at least forty years and remains experimental due to perceived unreliability, unclear safety limits and limited innovation. Suggestions for future research and standardisation are made throughout this review. If the technology is found to be a safe, effective and sustainable method of water purification, it may support Targets 6.1, 6.a and 6.b of the United Nations sustainable development goals.

1. Introduction
Water quality has been the cornerstone of public health for millennia, and municipal water treatment plants have existed for centuries []. Yet, there are still 411 million people who rely on untreated water and a further 1.8 billion who rely on basic or limited water treatment services. Unsafe practices result in approximately one million deaths per year, of which 395,000 are children under the age of five years []. Water scarcity and the burden of waterborne diseases are worsening due to growing industrial demand for water, industrial and agricultural pollution, population growth and climate change []. Typhoid, cholera, giardiasis, dysentery, bacterial gastroenteritis, hepatitis A and salmonellosis are the most common of these diseases. They are diarrhoeal, dehydrating, malnourishing, the second leading cause of child mortality, and more importantly, preventable [].

Water treatment in municipal treatment plants is a multi-stage process. Coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection are the core stages, though methods vary depending on the properties of intake water and the availability and affordability of chemicals, equipment and expertise. Downstream processes are reliant on coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation (CFS) to function effectively, so CFS is vital to public and environmental health. Aluminium salts and iron salts are premier chemical coagulants, but they are becoming increasingly unpopular in developing regions for several reasons. This is particularly true of aluminium sulphate (Al2(SO4)3), a.k.a. “alum” [].

Outside of municipal facilities, water treatment is often limited to traditional methods of filtration and disinfection, such as cloth filtration, sand filtration and solar disinfection (SODIS) []. Like their industrial counterparts, traditional methods of water treatment can also be improved with upstream CFS. CFS with chemical coagulants can be cost-prohibitive and convoluted for rural communities; securing a reliable supply of chemicals is also a common difficultly. As such, the adoption of natural, plant-based coagulants is being encouraged []. Natural coagulants can be grown locally to provide a cost effective and readily available supply of coagulant for CFS []. Jar testing is the standard laboratory method of assessing coagulants for CFS efficacy. Barring microbiological analysis, jar testing can be conducted inexpensively and with relatively little expertise []. Therefore, it is a remarkably accessible method of research, and the focus of this review.

Many plant materials have been identified as natural coagulants since the 1970s, with some having seen traditional use for over 2000 years []. The seeds of Moringa oleifera Lamarck (MO)—also known as the “drumstick tree”, “ben oil tree”, “miracle tree” or “tree of life”—have received the most attention to date []. MO is indigenous to Northern India and naturalised in tropical and subtropical regions of North America, South America, Africa, Asia and Australia. The propagation of MO can largely be attributed to the nutritional profile of its leaves and seed pods, the oil content of its seeds and medicinal properties reported in all parts of the plant. The adoption of MO as a drought-resistant source of food and medicine has been rapid, whereas its adoption as a natural coagulant is still experimental []. For the technology to progress beyond the experimental stage, research must be consistent and of a high standard.

The primary aim of this review was to assess the reliability of contemporary research (2014 – 2024) on water treatment with MO seed coagulants, with emphases on methodological consistency and standardisation. The secondary aim was to guide future research towards emerging theories, high-quality testing and unbiased reporting, so the technology can be trusted and progress. Both aims were achieved, and as of 2025, this is the only systematic review of this nature.

When the technology is determined to be safe, effective and sustainable, it can contribute to the United Nations (UN) sustainable development goals: Target 6.1 (“universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water”), Target 6.a (“expand international cooperation and capacity-building support to developing countries in water- and sanitation-related activities”) and Target 6.b (“support and strengthen the participation of local communities in improving water and sanitation management”). The UN aims to achieve these targets by 2030, so this technology must be researched promptly to contribute []. Additionally, the UN aims to accelerate the implementation of Goal 6 (Clean water and sanitation) by hosting a conference in December 2026 to discuss policy, financial resources, technologies and innovative tools []. By virtue of innovation and sustainability, natural coagulants may be of considerable interest to conference attendees.

2. Methodology of the systematic review
Academic databases and search engines (ScienceDirect, ResearchGate and Google Scholar) were selected for global accessibility and browsed using search terms (n = 21) created from combinations of prefix (n = 3) and suffix (n = 7) terms, as shown in Table 1.

3. Discussion

3.1. Background information

This section of the review provides pertinent information on alum and MO seed coagulants in context of low-income and rural communities in developing regions. An understanding of the advantages, disadvantages and mechanisms of action of these coagulants is used to support the assessments and recommendations made throughout the review. The systematic review of included reports begins in Section 3.2.

3.1.1. Advantages and disadvantages of aluminium sulphate.
Many publications summarise the disadvantages of chemical coagulants to promote the use of MO seeds. Alum is the most common chemical coagulant, so it is often used to typify aluminium salts in jar testing experiments. Other chemical coagulants, such as iron salts, are rarely tested alongside natural coagulants.

CFS with alum is known to acidify water [,,]; this effect is discussed in detail in Section 3.9.1. Water with lower pH (< 7) is more likely to corrode drinking water distribution systems []. To prevent corrosion, acidified water may require pH adjustment with alkaline chemicals, such as sodium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide or sodium carbonate []. This process requires equipment, expertise and a consistent supply of chemicals, which are not always available in rural and developing regions.

CFS with alum also produces environmentally-damaging, non-biodegradable sludge. Typically, alum sludge is dewatered to reduce volume and then dried by drainage and evaporation in sludge lagoons. Dry sludge is then transported to a landfill for disposal. Sludge lagoons require land and construction expertise to install []. In a life cycle assessment of alum and MO seed coagulant, Amante et al. [] found that 1 kg of alum consumed 41.6% more energy and produced 80.6% more carbon dioxide than 1 kg of processed MO seeds when both were dosed equally. Transportation of alum sludge accounted for 66.3% of alum’s energy consumption and 53.5% of its carbon dioxide emissions, demonstrating the economic and environmental impact of sludge disposal.

In addition to the compounding costs of production, import, pH adjustment and sludge disposal, a growing industrial demand for alum is increasing the chemical’s value and decreasing its availability. As a result, alum-treated drinking water is becoming more expensive and less reliable []. Unaffordable treated water can restrict lower-income households to untreated or inadequately-treated drinking water, resulting in disease. This was demonstrated in a 2016 study on water availability and cost in East Africa, whereby communally-supplied water was found to cost between 6% and 73% of the income of a six-person household, depending on treatment expenses [].

Unrelated to economic sustainability are concerns of neurological disease risk associated with drinking water treated with aluminium salts [,,]. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises this risk by recommending a safe residual aluminium salt concentration of < 0.9 mg/L in drinking water. They state that optimally-treated water contains aluminium salt concentrations of 0.1 – 0.2 mg/L []. As such, it can be inferred that residual aluminium salts in drinking water are only a risk to human health when CFS is conducted sub-optimally.

The advantages of alum are seldom discussed in context of natural coagulants, but they are worth mentioning to draw fair comparisons. With appropriate dosing (15 – 250 mg/L), alum is exceptionally effective, achieving turbidity and microbial load reductions of 95 – 99% [–,,,]. Unlike MO seed phytochemicals, alum is a single, consistent compound with well-understood properties and modes of action. As a result, standard operating procedures are readily available.

3.1.2. Advantages and disadvantages of M. oleifera seed coagulants.
As with alum and metal salts, MO seeds are often used as an exemplar when discussing natural coagulants. They are the most studied natural coagulant, they are often considered the most effective, and the MO tree is widely cultivated and trusted.

Unlike alum, MO seed coagulants are commonly reported as pH neutral [–,,,,,,]. As such, MO-treated waters are less likely to corrode drinking water distribution systems than alum-treated waters. See Section 3.9.1 for full pH data.

Unlike alum sludge, MO seed sludge is biodegradable and has been used as an agricultural fertiliser/pesticide hybrid. MO seeds contain chitin-binding proteins (Mo-CBPs), which exhibit fungicidal and insecticidal activity, hence their utility as a pesticide [–]. Due to the low macronutrient content and variable microbial load of MO seed sludge, Feria et al. [] recommend using it as a soil improver rather than as a fertiliser. Alternatively, they recommend treating the sludge with ≥ 3% hydrated lime to eliminate pathogens prior to use with crops. It should also be noted that MO seed coagulants are effective at removing heavy metals from contaminated water []. Heavy metals are known for their toxicity and ecotoxicity, so MO seed sludge should be treated as hazardous waste if heavy metal contamination is known or suspected.

If MO seed sludge cannot be used productively, its volume can be reduced in a sludge lagoon to minimise landfill expenses. Mosquitos breed in lagoons and mosquito-borne diseases, such as malaria, dengue fever and chikungunya, are leading causes of morbidity and mortality in tropical regions. As such, it is common practice to treat sludge lagoons and other bodies of standing water with larvicidal chemicals (or diesel fuel). Fortunately, the insecticidal activities of MO seeds extend to mosquito larvae, with LC50 values of 200 – 2500 mg/L [,]. A typical dose for MO seed coagulants is 2.5 – 350 mg/L and MO seed sludge volumes are reportedly as low as < 1% []. Assuming trace residual coagulant in the clarified water, it is theorised that MO seed concentrations can be as high as 250 – 35,000 mg/L in sludges; high enough to incur larvicidal activity and prevent mosquito breeding. Resultantly, lagoons with MO seed sludge may not require treatment with larvicidal chemicals, saving an additional expense. This theory requires additional research.

Outside of water treatment, MO seeds have also been appraised as a natural mosquito larvicide, whereby large quantities of MO seed powder can be administered to bodies of water to prevent mosquito breeding. While promising, non-target organisms (including predators of mosquito larvae) are killed by this action, so it is not recommended []. For this reason, MO seed sludge should be stored in purpose-built lagoons and not dumped into pre-existing bodies of water.

A publication from 1995 found MO seed sludge to be “four to five times less in volume than the chemical sludge produced by alum” []. This statistic is regularly quoted, but alum and MO seed sludge volumes are rarely measured in contemporary jar test publications. Low sludge volume is advantageous, as it reduces energy consumption and carbon dioxide emissions during sludge transportation. When MO seed sludge is applied locally as a fertiliser, pesticide or soil improver, transportation routes can be shorter, further lowering the economic and environmental impact of water treatment. In Amante et al.‘s [] life cycle assessment, MO seed sludge transportation consumed 33.3% less energy and produced 33.3% less CO2 than alum sludge transportation; MO seed sludge and alum sludge were transported 50 km and 75 km, respectively. Presumably, agricultural land can be found adjacent to rural communities in many instances, further lowering transportation costs.

Contrary to the compounding expenses of alum, MO seeds are inexpensive to grow and process, pH neutral and may produce sludge which can be disposed of locally and productively. Therefore, CFS with MO seed coagulants can be more cost-effective, less labour intensive and less environmentally damaging than CFS with chemical coagulants. The sum of these benefits is more affordable treated drinking water.

Secondary to the advantages of MO seed coagulants over chemical coagulants are the advantages of MO seed coagulants over other natural coagulants. MO is a drought-resistance tree that is widely naturalised in regions prone to drought and water scarcity. As such, it has a reputation for utility in drought and disaster relief, earning the common names “miracle tree”, “tree from heaven” and “God’s tree”. Some researchers dislike these monikers, but it is important to remember that they indicate trust, and trust is one of the key advantages of MO as a coagulant source. In Bancessi et al.’s [] trial of MO seed usage in Guinea-Bissau, 93% of participants were satisfied with MO seed teabags and 94% said they would recommend them to others. Participants demonstrated nutritional and medicinal knowledge of MO, and were eager to learn water treatment techniques involving the tree. After a week of usage, 94% of households believed it was important to treat water with MO seeds, and the same percentage said they would continue doing so. Some households mentioned “an abundance” of MO trees in their vicinity, enabling continued usage.

Often reported alongside the tangible benefits of MO seed coagulants are the nutritional and medicinal benefits of other MO plant materials. To summarise, antacid, anti-arthritic, anti-asthmatic, anti-atherosclerotic, anticancer, antidiabetic, anti-epileptic, anti-hypertensive, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-malarial, anti-ulcer, blood sugar balancing, cholesterol lowering and neuroprotective properties have all been studied in MO-derived materials []. While these properties explain trust in the tree, they should not be considered benefits of MO seed CFS. A goal of CFS is to minimise residual coagulant in post-treatment water; residual coagulant is therefore undesirable, as discussed in the following paragraphs.

Moving on to the disadvantages of MO seed coagulants, concerns about residual dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in treated water are common. Regarding acceptability, residual DOC can alter the taste, odour and colour of drinking water. In Bancessi et al.‘s [] trial, 51% of participants reported cloudiness and 58% reported a sweet taste in water treated with MO seed teabags (100 mg/L). Despite this, only 6% of households said they would not use them again, suggesting a low impact on drinking water acceptability. Regarding performance, residual DOC increases post-treatment turbidity, thereby decreasing CFS efficacy. Coagulant overdose exacerbates this problem, and low-turbidity intake water is particularly susceptible to this effect. Regarding safety, residual DOC is thought to decrease the shelf life of drinking water by enabling the regrowth of microorganisms [,]. In Bancessi et al.’s [] trial, 74% of participants said they consume water as soon as they collected it from a well, so the demand for drinking water with a long shelf life was not high in rural Guinea-Bissau. A second safety concern of residual DOC is the potential for disinfection by-products (DBPs). DBPs emerge when organic and inorganic residues react with chemical disinfectants. Chlorination of DOC and insoluble lipids from MO seed coagulants can produce harmful DBPs, such as trihalomethanes [,,]. This concern can be relieved by using alternative disinfectants, such as peracetic acid, and alternative methods of disinfection, such as SODIS [,]; for disinfection of saline waters, performic acid can be used to minimize DBP formation []. Unfortunately, Bancessi et al. [] found that the application of chlorine has increased due to misinformation surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic. In their trial, 39% of households reported everyday use of bleach to treat drinking water. Considering these disadvantages, a common trend in contemporary research can be discussed: many researchers are moving away from trialling whole MO seed powder (a.k.a. MO seed flour, raw MO seed, unrefined MO seed, etc.) as it is thought to increase residual DOC and lipids to unsatisfactory concentrations. The extraction of lipids (a.k.a. defatting, oil extraction, oil pressing, etc.) and the isolation of coagulant proteins via solubility fractionation are experimental methods of reducing DBP potential.

A disadvantage of MO usage that is rarely discussed is the risk the tree poses as an invasive species. MO is regarded as “potentially invasive or moderately invasive in tropical regions of the world.” The trees spread slowly but persistently, forming dense thickets. These characteristics suggest MO will pose a “long-term threat to certain natural habitats”, meaning its status as an invasive species may evolve over time []. In developing regions, the benefits of MO cultivation outweigh concerns of invasiveness, so the tree is commonly described as naturalised.

Another disadvantage of MO seeds is their inconsistent chemical profile. CFS capacity in natural coagulants is dependent on protein content, and protein content is affected by several factors. MO has numerous cultivars, some of which have been selectively bred for increased leaf biomass, seed pod biomass or oil yields. Geographic, environmental and seasonal conditions are also known to affect the chemical profile of MO trees [,]. Additionally, the storage time and storage conditions of MO seeds can have a large impact on CFS capacity. Shelf life of whole MO seeds was not tested in any of the included reports, but further reading suggests a shelf life of 3 – 24 months [,]. Inconsistent chemical profiles are inherent in plant materials, so natural coagulants will always be less reliable than chemical coagulants. To compensate, jar testing research requires a high degree of standardisation.

A final consideration for MO seed coagulants is the potential for toxicity and allergenicity. These disadvantages are largely neglected in contemporary jar testing reports, but they are being investigated with increasing frequency in toxicology, pharmacology and biochemistry journals. Toxicology is beyond the scope of this review, but independent research on this topic is encouraged.

3.1.3. Mechanisms of action of M. oleifera seed coagulants.
Colloidal materials and microorganisms are negatively charged and remain suspended in water indefinitely by electrostatic repulsion, as shown in Fig 2A. As a result, gravitational settling cannot exclude them to produce clean and safe drinking water []. This is particularly true of motile microorganisms, which can also overcome gravity using flagella and cilia [,]. The causative agents of several common waterborne diseases are motile, including Salmonella spp., Vibrio cholera, Escherichia coli and Campylobacter spp. [–]. Common non-motile waterborne pathogens include the infective cysts of Giardia duodenalis (a.k.a. G. intestinalis and G. lamblia), Shigella spp. and Hepatovirus A [–].

3.2. Effects of test water type and clouding agent usage

Test water type varied depending on the needs of the target population. Local rivers, lakes and reservoirs were sampled in 11 of 25 reports, reflecting the needs of people who rely on surface waters [,,–,,,,,,]. Waters from these sources had pH readings of 6.5 – 8.7 and turbidity readings of 5 – 210 NTU. The treatment of wastewaters is also a priority in developing regions, as the disposal of untreated wastewaters pollutes an estimated 5,500 billion m3 of water per year, exacerbating water scarcity and causing environmental damage. Additionally, treated wastewaters can be used for productive purposes, such as crop irrigation []. Wastewaters were sampled in 4 of 25 reports, and had pH readings of 5.1 – 8.5 and turbidity readings of 180 – 350 NTU [,,,]. Chales et al. [] used well water, with pH 7.1 and 200 NTU turbidity. Irikannu et al. [] used borehole water and sachet water with respective pH values of 6.72 – 6.95 and 6.73 – 6.98; this report tested total dissolved solids (TDS), but not turbidity or total suspended solids. Adesina et al. [] used surface water with pH 7.97 and “> 800 NTU” turbidity; the reason for an inexact turbidity reading is unclear. Kenea et al. [] and Ng & Elshikh [] did not report pre-treatment turbidity, so there experiments were neither replicable nor transparent. Both reports received “lowest quality” judgements and concerns of bias.

In absence of authentic test waters, 7 of 25 reports used synthetic water prepared from tap water or deionised water, with the addition of a clouding agent (e.g., kaolin, terracotta clay, soil). Turbidity in synthetic waters was dynamic and pH was typically neutral or near-neutral [,,,,,,]. The use of synthetic water is advised against when conducting microbiological testing, as residual disinfectants in tap water and low osmolarity in deionised water can damage microbial recovery rates [,]. Synthetic water may also be inadequate for DOC, TDS, biological oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) research, as discussed in Section 3.9.2.

In 7 of 25 reports, kaolin was used to adjust pre-treatment turbidity and increase colloidal load [,,,,,,]. Kaolin originates from the clay–mineral kaolinite, which is the dominant clay-sized mineral in tropical and subtropical soils []. It is a pervasive cause of turbidity and colour in surface and well waters, so it is an authentic choice for turbidity adjustment in jar testing. Five reports used a kaolin “stock suspension” for turbidity adjustment, to ensure complete hydration of kaolin particles and a high colloidal load with which to challenge MO seed coagulants [,,,,]. This was performed by adding kaolin to distilled water (e.g., 10 g in 500 ml), stirring the suspension for 10 – 60 minutes, and allowing non-colloidal particles to settle out, typically overnight. Test waters were then dosed with the supernatant of this suspension to adjust turbidity to desirable readings. When prepared this way, untreated control samples experienced minimal reductions in turbidity due to gravitational settling (0 – 19%) during jar testing. Shah et al. [,] were the exception to this, reporting turbidity reduction rates due to gravitational settling (i.e., 0 mg/L coagulant) of 66.9 – 84.9% in their first publication and 57.9 – 81.7% in their second publication. Their kaolin suspension “was prepared using 20 g of kaolin powder hand-stirred in tap water and left to settle overnight” and subsequently “stirred at 600 RMP for 10 min”. This suggests Shah et al. [,] did not dose test waters with the colloidal supernatant of the stock suspension, as indicated in other reports.

In tests where the kaolin stock suspension method was not used, gravitational settling typically caused turbidity reduction rates of 25 – 60% [,,,,]. In untreated wastewaters, turbidity reduction due to gravitational settling was as high as 70 – 80% [,]. Camacho et al. [] and Gaikwad & Munavalli [] used soil to adjust pre-treatment turbidity: the former reported turbidity reduction rates of 41 – 50% in untreated control samples following 60 – 120 min of sedimentation; the latter reported turbidity reduction rates of 0% in untreated controls, suggesting mathematical adjustment of data. Likewise, two additional research groups reported 0% turbidity reduction in untreated control samples [,]. It is unclear whether these values are legitimate or are obscuring gravitational settling rates to heighten the perceived efficacy of MO seed coagulants. In addition, 5 of 25 reports did not include negative control data, so the magnitude of gravitational settling could not always be determined [,,,,]. Addich et al. [] and Adesina et al. [] received “high risk of bias” judgements for this reason. The former tested with wastewater and the latter tested with “>800 NTU” surface water, so significant gravitational settling was expected in both instances. Missing data of this type can lead to an overestimation of treatment efficacy, and was therefore a common cause of bias concern. Missing and questionable control data also impacted research quality. To facilitate standardisation, kaolin is the recommended clouding agent when turbidity adjustment is necessary. The inclusion of full, unadjusted control data is also encouraged.

A final consideration for kaolin usage is the mineral’s colour. Refined kaolin, MO seed coagulants and alum are all white in colour; therefore, visual observations of CFS in synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters can be difficult to make. This is particularly true when assessing the impact of coagulant overdose, whereby two mechanisms exist. The first mechanism occurs when suspended solids (Fig 3A) are saturated with a coagulant and the excess coagulant has no surface to adsorb to (Fig 3B). During sedimentation, neutral complexes settle out of suspension, leaving behind positively charged excess coagulant. Via electrostatic repulsion, excess coagulant remains in suspension and is incorporated into potable water or downstream stages of treatment. The second mechanism (Fig 3C) is called “resuspension”, “restabilisation” or “charge reversal”, and occurs when suspended solids are oversaturated with coagulant. As a result, colloid–coagulant complexes become positively charged and remain in suspension via electrostatic repulsion. In this scenario, coagulant and colloids are incorporated into potable water or downstream stages of treatment [,]. Resuspension is an unsafe outcome for CFS as the colloid fraction may include pathogens, toxic heavy metals or other harmful substances. Additionally, both mechanisms of overdose increase residual coagulant concentrations, which can increase turbidity and DOC and reduce drinking water acceptability.

3.3. Effects of M. oleifera seed age and storage conditions

MO seeds were sourced domestically in 17 of 25 reports, demonstrating the wide availability of the plant [,–,–,–,,–]. Researchers in Denmark, South Korea and the United Kingdom sourced their MO seeds from Brazil, India and Pakistan, respectively [,,,]. Four research groups did not state the source of their MO seeds [,,,].

Freitas et al. [] and Taiwo et al. [] verified the species of their seeds with a herbarium and botanist, respectively. This practice should be considered in future research, particularly when researchers cannot harvest seed themselves and rely on external suppliers or vendors.

Petersen et al. [] and Shah et al. [] were the only researchers to disclose the age of their MO seeds at testing; they were ~1 month old and 2 – 3 months old, respectively. Seed age is an important variable to disclose as the CFS capacity of MO seeds has been shown to diminish 3 – 24 months after harvest [,]. This variable can be considered a confounding factor, as it can affect an independent variable (MOCP concentration) and a dependant variable (treatment efficacy) simultaneously. Failure to declare MO seed age was a common risk of bias concern.

Three research groups stored their seeds at room temperature [,,]. Baptista et al. [] refrigerated their seeds prior to use, so there was evidence of inconsistent storage conditions, although storage temperature was not found to impact CFS capacity in a 2006 report []. Afzal et al. [] reported significantly higher protein content in seeds stored in hermetic storage bags than in seeds stored in cloth bags at 10°C (283.2 K) and 25°C (298.2 K). They also reported that seeds with 8% moisture content retained higher protein concentrations than seeds with 10 – 12% moisture content. To preserve cationic protein content and CFS capacity, seeds can be air-dried prior to storage and stored in air-tight containers to prevent the reuptake of moisture. Reporting seed age and storage conditions should be considered standard practice.

3.4. Preparation of coagulants from M. oleifera seed

As with the preparation of test waters, methods for preparing MO seed coagulants varied depending on the needs of the target population. Based on the complexity and expense of MOCP extraction, methods can be categorised as “primary processing”, “secondary processing” and “tertiary processing” [,]. Processing stages are sequential, as shown in Fig 4; secondary processing cannot be conducted without primary processing, and tertiary processing cannot be conducted without primary and secondary processing.

3.5. Effects of MO seed coagulant dosing concentrations

MO seed coagulants were dosed at 2.5 – 350 mg/L in 16 of 25 reports [,,,,,,,–,]. Active MOCP concentrations vary between preparation methods, so correlations between pre-treatment turbidity, coagulant dose and turbidity reduction rate could not be established. For example, Delelegn et al. [] achieved 83.8% turbidity reduction in 208 NTU water using MO seed powder at 16 mg/L, and Chales et al. [] achieved 89.5% turbidity reduction in 200 NTU water using a defatted saline extract at 5 mg/L. However, Petersen et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction of 91.7% in 150 – 175 NTU water using a whole-seed aqueous extract at 200 mg/L. In these examples, pre-treatment turbidity readings and turbidity reduction rates were comparable, whereas optimal dosing concentrations varied significantly depending on the coagulant preparation methods and resultant concentrations of available MOCPs. As such, researchers should aim to trial MO seed coagulants at dynamic concentrations instead of relying on static doses from pre-existing publications. Even when processing methods are carried out identically, varying phytochemical profiles can affect MOCP concentration in unpredictable ways.

In 5 of 25 reports, MO seed coagulants were tested at concentrations higher than the common range of 2.5 – 350 mg/L. Jung et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 95% in 325 NTU wastewater using whole-seed aqueous extracts at 500 mg/L, and Addich et al. [] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 87.5% in 200 NTU wastewater using MO seed powder at 600 mg/L. Using computational modelling, Adesina et al. [] predicted a turbidity reduction of 99.3% in “> 800 NTU” water using a whole-seed aqueous extract at 3,000 mg/L; the accuracy of this model was reportedly verified via jar testing. Ng & Elshikh [] reported turbidity reduction rates of 94.9% using a defatted saline extract at 20,000 mg/L; pre-treatment turbidity was not reported, so it was unclear why elevated dosing concentrations were chosen in this instance. Due to the high risk of bias associated with Addich et al. [] and Adesina et al.’s [] reports, the utility of elevated coagulant dosing cannot be reliably assessed.

In one report, dosing concentration was unclear due to imprecise language such as “small quantity of clean water” and “two drops [of coagulant]” []. In a second report, dosing concentration was unclear because jar test volume was not reported and coagulant dose was consistently reported in “mg” and not “mg/L” []. Both reports received “lowest quality” judgements as they were not replicable. To enable replicability, precise measurements are necessary and encouraged.

Data pertaining to MO seed coagulant dosing ranges, optimal doses and treatment efficacy are displayed in Table 15. To investigate potential correlations between these variables, data from Table 15 was plotted onto three scatter graphs. No significant correlations were observed between pre-treatment turbidity and optimal coagulant dose (Fig 5), pre-treatment turbidity and optimal turbidity reduction rate (Fig 6) or optimal coagulant dose and optimal turbidity reduction rate (Fig 7). Pre-treatment turbidity values were unclear in several reports, so it was not possible to include every data set from Table 15 in these graphs. Therefore, the Figs 5–7 should be considered exploratory and not definitive.

3.6. Effects of chemical coagulant dosing concentrations

Arguments for the adoption of natural coagulants are largely responses to the shortcomings of chemical coagulants, with particular emphasis on alum. As such, alum was selected as a positive control in 8 of 25 reports. With appropriate dosing, alum is an effective and consistent coagulant: Amante et al. [] achieved 97.9% turbidity reduction in 53 NTU synthetic water using alum at 100 mg/L; Chales et al. [] achieved 98.0% turbidity reduction in 200 NTU well water using alum at 20 mg/L; Delelegn et al. [] achieved 98.4 – 99.1% turbidity reduction in 129 NTU and 208 NTU river waters using alum at 16 mg/L; Hounsinou et al. [] achieved ~95% turbidity reduction in 40 NTU lake water using alum at 40 mg/L, and; Shah et al. [,] achieved turbidity reduction rates of 98.4 – 99.2% in 82 NTU synthetic water using alum at 30 – 250 mg/L.

Conversely, inappropriate dosing can result in the misleading notion that alum is an ineffective coagulant. By extrapolation, this can lead to an overestimation of MO seed coagulant utility. Taiwo et al. [] demonstrated 19.1% turbidity reduction in 41 NTU reservoir water using alum at 5% w/v (50,000 mg/L) and Freitas et al. [] demonstrated 56.5% turbidity reduction in 38 NTU river water using alum at 2% w/v (20,000 mg/L). Both reports received “high risk of bias” judgements for this reason. As a guideline, appropriate dosing ranges for alum and MO seed coagulants were broadly comparable at 5 – 250 mg/L and 2.5 – 350 mg/L, respectively.

Hendrawati et al. [] were the only researchers to use an alternative to alum, employing polyaluminum chloride (PAC) as a positive control. At 100 mg/L, PAC and MO seed powder achieved respective turbidity reduction rates of 89.4 – 89.6% and 97.4 – 98.6% in both wastewater (320 – 350 NTU) and groundwater (220 – 230 NTU). In this instance, the natural coagulant outperformed the chemical coagulant at an identical dose. For tabulated data on chemical coagulant dosing, see Table 16.

3.10. Methods of data analysis

Methods of statistical analysis were disclosed in 20 of 25 reports. Twelve used mean values ± standard deviation, analysis of variance (ANOVA) and/or Tukey’s test at 95% confidence [–,,,,,,,]. Three research groups used response surface methodology [,,]. Petersen et al. [] used a normal linear regression model, validated by quantile–quantile plots and a residual plot; the model was reduced by backward stepwise regression at 95% confidence. Five reports did not disclose analytical methods [,,,,]. Missing methodological data was commonly associated with “lower quality” and “lowest quality” judgements and increased risk of bias.

4. Summary of findings

- The systematic review was completed to PRISMA 2020 standards using Cochrane tools modified for in vitro laboratory studies. The reliability of contemporary research was assessed and many recommendations were made to guide future research towards high-quality, unbiased testing and emerging theories; the aims of the review were therefore completed.

- The scope of the systematic review was limited due to its small research team and budget. Screening was limited to the first ten results for each search term (n = 21) within each search year (2014 – 2024) in each academic database and search engine used (n = 3); toll access reports were also excluded from data collection. Nonetheless, 25 jar testing reports were included, from which 511 data points were collected and synthesised.

- The reliability of contemporary jar testing with MO seed coagulants was inconsistent. Research quality assessments returned nine “highest quality” or “higher quality” judgments and 16 “lower quality” or “lowest quality” judgements. Risk of bias assessments returned seven “low risk of bias” judgements, 12 “some concerns” judgements, and six “high risk of bias” judgements. Reports with “high risk of bias” judgements were found to underestimate the efficacy of CFS with MO seed coagulants.

- The most concerning findings were inadequate reporting of negative control data in 8 of 25 reports, absent positive control data in 16 of 25 reports, inappropriate positive control dosing concentrations in two reports, and failure to declare the age of MO seeds (a confounding factor) in 23 of 25 reports.

- MO seeds retained high CFS capacity when they were dried prior to storage and stored in air-tight containers to prevent the reuptake of moisture. Drying temperatures exceeding 90°C (363.2 K) damaged CFS capacity.

- Methods of coagulant processing can be categorised as primary (MO seed powders), secondary (MO seed extracts) and tertiary (purified MOCPs). Powders were studied in 9 of 25 reports, extracts were studied 18 of 25 and purified protein was studied in one report. Extracts were typically aqueous (n = 15) or saline (n = 6).

- Saline extracts commonly outperformed aqueous extracts, and aqueous extracts rarely outperformed MO seed powders when tested in parallel. This is theoretically a result of MOCP self-association in aqueous extracts and modulation of protein–protein interactions in saline extracts; this theory requires additional research.

- Due to their comparable molecular masses, occurrence as oligomers, tendency to self-associate, thermostability, and affinity for carbohydrate and chitin binding, MOCPs are believed to be lectins with hevein-like binding domains.

- MO seed coagulants were commonly tested at 2.5 – 350 mg/L. Overdose can result in the suspension of excess coagulant and possible resuspension of colloids and pathogens. There was no consensus optimum dose because MOCP concentrations vary between seed batches and methods of processing.

- CFS with MO seed coagulants consistently achieved turbidity reduction rates of 80 – 96% when the three-stage model of CFS was adhered to. Deviation from the three-stage model was the predominant cause of ineffective CFS. Modal operating parameters were: coagulation at 100 RPM for 2 min, flocculation 20 RPM for 15 min, and sedimentation at 0 RPM for 60 min.

- CFS with alum achieved turbidity reduction rates of 95.0 – 99.2% when dosed optimally (16 – 250 mg/L). As such, alum commonly outperformed MO seed coagulants.

- CFS with alum was reported to acidify water, whereas CFS with MO seed coagulants was reportedly pH neutral. These reports were verified by contemporary publications.

- CFS with alum was also reported to produce high volumes of toxic sludge, whereas CFS with MO seed coagulants was reported to produce low volumes of biodegradable sludge. Sludges are not being studied in contemporary publications, so these reports could not be verified or refuted.

- When DOC, BOD and COD experiments were performed with authentic test waters, MO seed coagulants reduced oxidisable residue concentrations significantly. When synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters were used, MO seed coagulants increased oxidisable residue concentrations.

- Microbiological testing was uncommon and focussed primarily on coliforms and E. coli. Correlations between microbial load reduction and turbidity reduction were found in three reports, whereas two reports demonstrated no significant correlation. Microbiological methodologies were occasionally flawed.

4.1. Recommendations

- Future research can benefit from improved standardisation and data reporting practices. To test the theory that MO seed coagulants are viable alternatives to chemical coagulants, both natural and chemical coagulants must be tested in parallel. To demonstrate CFS is more effective than gravitational settling, tests must contain untreated negative control samples (i.e., 0 mg/L coagulant). Full data must be reported for both positive and negative controls.

- Standardisation can also be improved by reporting MO seed age and storage conditions, adhering to the three-stage model of CFS and adhering to the common coagulant dosing range. Standardisation assists the research community in identifying causes of favourable and unfavourable results by reducing the range of independent variables and impact of confounding factors.

- Primary-processed coagulants are practical for use in rural sub-Saharan Africa, the region most affected by economic water scarcity and energy poverty. Whole-seed MO powder should not be neglected in favour of secondary-processed extracts and defatting, which can be impractical and economically unviable when prepared using complexed methods and electrical equipment. When testing extracts, consider testing MO seed powder in parallel as a control measure; extracts do not always outperform dry powder.

- Sludge disposal is a major expense of CFS, so sludge research requires more attention than it is currently receiving. Measuring and comparing sludge volumes in waters treated with MO seed coagulants and chemical coagulants is a simple way to contribute to sludge research.

- DOC, BOD, COD and TDS experiments are best performed with authentic test waters. Synthetic and turbidity-adjusted waters can have atypically low pre-treatment organic load, particularly when inorganic clouding agents, such as kaolin, are used. Measuring dissolved residues in non-authentic waters may return misleading results.

- Researchers with adequate facilities should strive to include microbiological measurements in their jar testing experiments to expand the currently-limited evidence base. Where health and safety permits it, alternate waterborne pathogens should also be trialled to ensure effective microbial load reduction with non-coliform organisms. Synthetic water (i.e., tap water, distilled water) is not suitable for microbiological testing.

If researchers wish to participate in standardised jar testing with MO seed coagulants, consider the reporting criteria and suggestions listed in Table 18. The reporting criteria in Table 18 may also benefit researchers working on alternate natural coagulants.

title: Association of erythropoietin gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C>T/G) with diabetic retinopathy in Type 2 diabetes mellitus patients of Punjabi population in Pakistan
content:
Abstract
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and is influenced by genetic factors. We investigated the association between the erythropoietin (EPO) gene polymorphism (rs1617640 C > T/G) and DR risk in a Punjabi Pakistani cohort of adults with T2DM. In a case–control design, 573 T2DM patients (294 with DR, 279 controls without retinopathy, CDR) were genotyped by ARMS-PCR. The protective CC genotype was significantly more frequent in controls (96.77%) than in cases (30.61%) and was associated with markedly reduced DR risk (OR = 68; 95% CI 33.468–138.162; p < 0.001). Conversely, the GG and TT genotypes were absent in controls but present in DR patients (27.55% and 21.43%, respectively) and were strongly associated with increased DR risk (p < 0.001). Allele-level analysis mirrored genotype findings: the C allele predominated in controls (98.39%) but was significantly less frequent in cases (39%), while G and T alleles were enriched among DR patients (p < 0.001). Together, genotype- and allele-based results indicate that the rs1617640 C variant is protective against DR in this Punjabi T2DM population, whereas G and T variants increase DR susceptibility.
